data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"On clear, calm nights, the nocturnal UHI is dominated by a longwave radiation trap caused by dense urban geometry, and the cross-city magnitude of this effect scales with built density and building height because these factors decrease the sky view factor, impeding radiative cooling.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If urban geometry is characterized by wide, open avenues with high sky view factors, the radiation trap mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cloud cover is uniform, it replaces the sky view factor as the dominant limiter of longwave cooling, erasing geometric differences.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speeds are high, turbulent mixing replaces radiative cooling as the dominant nocturnal heat removal process.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Tall buildings and narrow street canyons restrict the view of the cold sky, trapping longwave radiation emitted by the urban surface and preventing efficient nocturnal cooling. Cities with denser, taller building configurations exhibit stronger UHI effects because the reduced sky view factor further delays the release of stored heat, keeping the urban canopy warmer.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
